newsitem.title: FRANCE: EU centrists insist on Amsterdam EMU pact signing.
newsitem.headline: EU centrists insist on Amsterdam EMU pact signing.

text.p: European Union centrist politicians insisted on Tuesday that France's problem with the EMU stability pact should be overcome at an EU summit next week.

Meeting ahead of the summit in Amsterdam next Monday and Tuesday, leaders of the mainly Christian Democrat European People's Party (EPP) said the impasse in their plans caused by France had to be sorted out.
They also said the new EU treaty must be completed and signed at the summit.
"I hope the French find the courage to finalise their position before the Amsterdam summit," Luxembourg Prime Minister Jean-Claude Juncker told reporters.
Wilfried Martens, president of the EPP, dismissed talk of an extra summit to deal with the impasse.
"We want it to be signed as it stands by the 15 European governments (in Amsterdam)," he said after the meeting which grouped the leaders of Germany, France, Belgium and Luxembourg.
Spain was represented by its foreign minister, Abel Matutes, who had earlier said a second summit could not be excluded if there was no deal in Amsterdam.

At a meeting in Luxembourg on Monday, French Finance Minister Dominique Strauss-Kahn told his EU partners that Paris needed time to study the stability pact, an integral part of plans for economic and monetary union (EMU).
He said the earliest date that the National Assembly could be consulted was June 19.
The pact, agreed in principle in Dublin in December, is designed to keep EU budgets in order after EMU is launched on January 1, 1999.
The European Commission is rushing to find a way to meet France's concerns, which revolve around its view that job creation should play a more important role in the EU's EMU plans.
Commission President Jacques Santer, who attended the EPP meeting, is expected to offer France a two-point plan when he visits Paris on Thursday.
It will suggest that two resolutions be attached to the stability pact, one on economic policy coordination, the other on employment policy coordination.
France believes more attention must be paid to job creation and that governments must have a large role in monetary policy when the single currency is introduced on January 1, 1999.
